world.bio: Second-generation laksa hawker at a Toa Payoh hawker centre. My father started the stall in 1978; I took over in 1999. I still pound the rempah by hand every Monday, and I sell about 180 bowls on a weekday. My daughter wants to go to culinary school abroad and I have no idea how those applications work or what they cost.
skills_assets: A stall in the Toa Payoh hawker centre, with a regular crowd of about 40 customers
The family laksa recipe, including a hand-pounded rempah that takes four hours
A stone mortar and pestle my father bought in 1980
Long relationships with the cockle, tau pok and fish cake suppliers
An old exercise book with all my accounts, written by hand

projects.name: Stall rent and tender
projects.text: The stall rent went up at the last tender, from $1,600 to $2,300 a month. I cut back on cockles and use fewer prawns. Some customers noticed and said nothing. I keep the price at $4.50 a bowl because I know the old ones count the coins.

projects.name: Daughter's culinary school plans
projects.text: Mei wants to study at a culinary school in Lyon or Singapore's ITE and then abroad. She has shown me a page of fees: tuition around forty thousand euros for a year, not counting living costs. I nodded as if I understood. I don't know what 'application portfolio' means or who writes the reference letters.

notes.text: Monday. Pounded rempah from 6am with my knee strapped up. The surgeon said I could stand for four hours, but at the stall I stand ten. By noon the knee is swollen like a bun. My daughter says I should hire someone. I said who will pound it the way my father taught me.

Sold 178 bowls. Not bad for a rainy Sunday. A tourist from Japan took a photo of the bowl and asked me what 'laksa leaf' was. I said 'daun kesum' and he wrote it down. I felt proud for a minute, then tired for the rest of the day.

Mei came home with a printout from a school in France. The tuition made my chest tighten. She said Papa, I will apply for scholarships. I said what scholarships. She said I'll find out. I looked at her and thought she is much braver than I was at her age.

Rent letter again: the new rate takes effect next month. I sat at the stall counting how many extra bowls I need to cover the difference: about thirty a month. Doable. But I am sixty and my knee is not.

Mahjong with old classmates on Sunday night. Won 12 dollars. Ah Hock complained about his son who refuses to take over his bak kut teh stall. I said at least yours is alive; my daughter wants to leave, but not because she hates the stall. She wants to learn how to cook for more than one bowl at a time. I understand that.
Physiotherapy appointment. The therapist says I should do the leg lifts every morning. I said I pound rempah. She said that's not a substitute. Maybe she is right.

Wrote down the family recipe in the exercise book for Mei. She asked why the measure for belachan is 'a thumb'. I said because my father's thumb was exactly that size. She laughed. I did not tell her that I am afraid nobody will ever make it like this.

A long weekend. Customers came earlier than usual. A little girl asked me if the laksa was spicy. I said only if you want it to be. She said 'I want it spicy!' Her mother looked terrified. I made it a medium.

messages.text:
Mei: Papa, can you come to the open day at the culinary school next month?
Me: Which day?
Mei: October 17th. It's at the campus, 2pm.
Me: I will ask my neighbour to take over the stall.

Auntie Pat: Did you see the new rent?
Me: Yes.
Auntie Pat: Everyone is moaning. Some want to leave.
Me: Where to? Nobody wants to leave a hawker centre in Toa Payoh.

Ah Hock: Mahjong Sunday?
Me: If my knee allows.
Ah Hock: It's mahjong, not marathon.
Me: Fine.

Supplier: Cockle price up 15 per cent.
Me: Again?
Supplier: Climate, they say.
Me: Then I will use fewer.

Wife: Did you eat?
Me: Yes, a bowl of my own.
Wife: Not enough. I made chicken rice, come home.
Me: Ten minutes.

calendar.event: Culinary school open day with Mei, 2pm

relations.about: Twenty-three, trained at a polytechnic, wants to go overseas to learn French cuisine.
Next stall, sells chicken rice, has the same rent worries.
Old classmate, plays mahjong, has a son who won't take over his stall.

constraints: Cannot leave the stall for more than a day
Not comfortable with online forms and English-language portals
sensitive: Afraid nobody will carry on the recipe
Savings are modest and tuition abroad looks impossible
Pride makes it hard to ask for help
